summary.text: Introduce the auxiliary sequence \(b_0=2, b_1=56\), \(b_{n+2}=-4b_{n+1}-64b_n\), and prove by induction the stronger overlapping identities \(a_{2n+1}=b_n^2\), \(a_{2n+2}=b_nb_{n+1}+64^{n+1}\), \(a_{2n+3}=b_{n+1}^2\), and \(a_{2n+4}=b_{n+1}b_{n+2}+64^{n+2}\). Substitution into the fourth-order recurrence, together with the recurrence for \(b\), advances this four-term window, and the first identity gives the required square.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(k\ge 0\),
\[
a_{k+4}=-4a_{k+3}+256a_{k+1}+4096a_k.
\]
We prove that \(a_{2n+1}\) is a square for every \(n\ge 0\).

Set \(q=64\), so that \(256=4q\) and \(4096=q^2\). Introduce an auxiliary integer sequence \((b_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
b_0=2,\qquad b_1=56,
\]
and
\[
b_{n+2}=-4b_{n+1}-q b_n
\tag{1}
\]
for every \(n\ge0\). We will prove the stronger collection of identities
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2n+1}&=b_n^2, \tag{2}\
a_{2n+2}&=b_n b_{n+1}+q^{n+1}, \tag{3}\
a_{2n+3}&=b_{n+1}^2, \tag{4}\
a_{2n+4}&=b_{n+1}b_{n+2}+q^{n+2}. \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
These four identities will be established simultaneously by induction on \(n\).

For \(n=0\), the first three are immediate from the initial values:
\[
a_1=4=2^2=b_0^2,
\]
\[
a_2=176=2\cdot56+64=b_0b_1+q,
\]
and
\[
a_3=3136=56^2=b_1^2.
\]
For the fourth identity, first use (1) to calculate
\[
b_2=-4b_1-qb_0=-4\cdot56-64\cdot2=-352.
\]
The recurrence for \(a_n\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_4
&=-4a_3+256a_1+4096a_0\\
&=-4\cdot3136+256\cdot4+4096(-1)\\
&=-15616.
\end{aligned}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
b_1b_2+q^2=56(-352)+64^2=-19712+4096=-15616.
\]
Thus (5) also holds when \(n=0\), completing the base case.

Now suppose that (2)--(5) hold for some fixed \(n\ge0\). To make the algebra transparent, write
\[
x=b_n,\qquad y=b_{n+1},\qquad z=b_{n+2}.
\]
By the auxiliary recurrence,
\[
z=-4y-qx.
\tag{6}
\]
The induction hypotheses become
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2n+1}&=x^2,\\
a_{2n+2}&=xy+q^{n+1},\\
a_{2n+3}&=y^2,\\
a_{2n+4}&=yz+q^{n+2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]
We first derive the next odd-indexed identity. Apply the recurrence for \(a\) with \(k=2n+1\):
\[
a_{2n+5}=-4a_{2n+4}+256a_{2n+2}+4096a_{2n+1}.
\]
Using \(256=4q\), \(4096=q^2\), and the identities in (7), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2n+5}
&=-4\bigl(yz+q^{n+2}\bigr)
  +4q\bigl(xy+q^{n+1}\bigr)+q^2x^2\\
&=-4yz+4qxy+q^2x^2
  +\bigl(-4q^{n+2}+4q\,q^{n+1}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
The two pure-power terms cancel because \(4q\,q^{n+1}=4q^{n+2}\). Hence
\[
a_{2n+5}=-4yz+4qxy+q^2x^2.
\]
Substituting \(z=-4y-qx\) from (6) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2n+5}
&=-4y(-4y-qx)+4qxy+q^2x^2\\
&=16y^2+8qxy+q^2x^2\\
&=(-4y-qx)^2\\
&=z^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
Thus
\[
a_{2n+5}=b_{n+2}^2.
\]
This is the new instance of the odd square identity.

It remains to derive the adjacent even-indexed identity needed to continue the induction. Put
\[
w=b_{n+3}.
\]
Applying the auxiliary recurrence one index later gives
\[
w=-4z-qy.
\tag{9}
\]
Now apply the recurrence for \(a\) with \(k=2n+2\):
\[
a_{2n+6}=-4a_{2n+5}+256a_{2n+3}+4096a_{2n+2}.
\]
Using (8), (7), and again \(256=4q\) and \(4096=q^2\), we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2n+6}
&=-4z^2+4qy^2+q^2\bigl(xy+q^{n+1}\bigr)\\
&=-4z^2+4qy^2+q^2xy+q^{n+3}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]
Here we used \(q^2q^{n+1}=q^{n+3}\). Equation (6) implies
\[
-qyz=-qy(-4y-qx)=4qy^2+q^2xy.
\tag{11}
\]
Substituting (11) into (10), and then using (9), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2n+6}
&=-4z^2-qyz+q^{n+3}\\
&=z(-4z-qy)+q^{n+3}\\
&=zw+q^{n+3}\\
&=b_{n+2}b_{n+3}+q^{n+3}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
\]

We can now verify all four assertions at \(n+1\). The first two are simply the third and fourth induction hypotheses, with their indices rewritten:
\[
a_{2(n+1)+1}=a_{2n+3}=b_{n+1}^2,
\]
and
\[
a_{2(n+1)+2}=a_{2n+4}=b_{n+1}b_{n+2}+q^{n+2}.
\]
The third assertion at \(n+1\) is exactly (8):
\[
a_{2(n+1)+3}=a_{2n+5}=b_{n+2}^2.
\]
Finally, the fourth assertion at \(n+1\) is (12):
\[
a_{2(n+1)+4}=a_{2n+6}=b_{n+2}b_{n+3}+q^{n+3}.
\]
Thus (2)--(5) hold at \(n+1\), and simultaneous induction proves them for every nonnegative integer \(n\).

In particular, the first identity (2) says that for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
a_{2n+1}=b_n^2.
\]
Since each \(b_n\) is an integer, every odd-indexed term \(a_{2n+1}\) is therefore a perfect square, as claimed.
